claim: The cellular enzymes that regulate the addition and removal of Kcr are unknown.
source: However, the cellular enzymes that regulate the addition and removal of Kcr are unknown, which has hindered further investigation of its cellular functions.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract, representing the state of knowledge at the time of the study.

claim: Sirt1, Sirt2, and Sirt3 can catalyze the hydrolysis of lysine crotonylated histone peptides and proteins.
source: We found that Sirt1, Sirt2, and Sirt3 can catalyze the hydrolysis of lysine crotonylated histone peptides and proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including LC-MS analyses showing hydrolysis of crotonylated peptides (Figure 4) and Western blot analyses showing decrotonylation of histone proteins (Figure 5).

claim: Sirt3 functions as a decrotonylase to regulate histone Kcr dynamics and gene transcription in living cells.
source: More importantly, Sirt3 functions as a decrotonylase to regulate histone Kcr dynamics and gene transcription in living cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that Sirt3 knockdown causes accumulation of histone crotonylation (Figure 5C, D) and affects gene transcription (Figure 5F).

claim: Histone PTMs play a crucial role in regulating a wide range of biological processes, such as gene transcription, DNA replication, and chromosome segregation.
source: Histone posttranslational modifications (PTMs) play a crucial role in regulating a wide range of biological processes, such as gene transcription, DNA replication, and chromosome segregation (Kouzarides, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kouzarides, 2007, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: PTMs of histones can serve as a heritable 'code' (so-called 'histone code'), which provides epigenetic information that a mother cell can pass to its daughters.
source: Increasing evidence has indicated that PTMs of histones can serve as a heritable 'code' (so-called 'histone code'), which provides epigenetic information that a mother cell can pass to its daughters (Jenuwein and Allis, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jenuwein and Allis, 2001, representing established scientific knowledge about the histone code hypothesis.

claim: Lysine acetylation (Kac) was among the first covalent modification of histones to be described.
source: Lysine acetylation (Kac) was among the first covalent modification of histones to be described (Allfrey and Mirsky, 1964; Allfrey et al., 1964).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Allfrey and Mirsky, 1964 and Allfrey et al., 1964, representing historical scientific knowledge.

claim: Histone Kac has been correlated with gene expression.
source: Since its identification, histone Kac has been correlated with gene expression.
evidence: This represents established scientific knowledge about the relationship between histone acetylation and gene expression.

claim: Kac plays an important role in controlling chromatin structure and gene transcription.
source: Extensive studies have now revealed that Kac plays an important role in controlling chromatin structure and gene transcription (Grunstein, 1997; Yang and Seto, 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Grunstein, 1997 and Yang and Seto, 2008a, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: By neutralizing positively charged lysine residues, acetylation alters the coulumbic interactions between basic histones and the negatively charged DNA, and thereby influences the structure of chromatin compaction.
source: By neutralizing positively charged lysine residues, acetylation alters the coulumbic interactions between basic histones and the negatively charged DNA, and thereby influences the structure of chromatin compaction (Ura et al., 1997; Shogren-Knaak et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ura et al., 1997 and Shogren-Knaak et al., 2006, representing established mechanistic understanding.

claim: Acetylation may serve as a docking site for 'reader' proteins (e.g., bromodomain containing proteins), which are recruited onto chromatin to carry out downstream cellular processes, such as gene transcription.
source: In addition, acetylation may serve as a docking site for 'reader' proteins (e.g., bromodomain containing proteins), which are recruited onto chromatin to carry out downstream cellular processes, such as gene transcription (Dhalluin et al., 1999; Marmorstein and Berger, 2001; Zeng et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dhalluin et al., 1999, Marmorstein and Berger, 2001, and Zeng et al., 2010, representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: In postmeiotic male germ cells, Kcr specifically marks testis specific X-linked genes, suggesting it is likely that it is an important histone mark for male germ cell differentiation.
source: In postmeiotic male germ cells, Kcr specifically marks testis specific X-linked genes, suggesting it is likely that it is an important histone mark for male germ cell differentiation.
evidence: This claim combines a factual observation (Kcr marks testis specific X-linked genes) with a speculative interpretation about its importance for male germ cell differentiation.

claim: HDAC3 in complex with nuclear receptor corepressor 1 (HDAC3–NCoR1) had detectable decrotonylase activity towards a model peptide substrate in a fluorometric assay.
source: In a systematic screening of the activities of the 11 human zinc-dependent lysine deacetylases (i.e., HDAC1–HDAC11) against a series of C-terminal lysine acylated peptides, Olsen et al. found that HDAC3 in complex with nuclear receptor corepressor 1 (HDAC3–NCoR1) had detectable decrotonylase activity towards a model peptide substrate in a fluorometric assay (Madsen and Olsen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Madsen and Olsen, 2012, describing prior work.

claim: Sirt1 and Sirt2 can catalyze the removal of a crotonyl group from a histone H3K9Cr peptide.
source: Recently, using a radioactive thin layer chromatography based assay, Denu et al. demonstrated that Sirt1 and Sirt2 can catalyze the removal of a crotonyl group from a histone H3K9Cr peptide (Feldman et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Feldman et al., 2013, describing prior work.

claim: A Cross-Linking Assisted and Stable isotope labeling of amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) based Protein Identification (CLASPI) approach has recently been reported to identify histone PTM 'readers'.
source: A Cross-Linking Assisted and Stable isotope labeling of amino acids in cell culture (SILAC) based Protein Identification (CLASPI) approach has recently been reported to identify histone PTM 'readers' (Li et al., 2012; Li and Kapoor, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2012 and Li and Kapoor, 2010, describing prior work.

claim: The CLASPI approach has not previously been explored to identify histone PTM 'erasers', which are likely involved in weak and transient interactions.
source: However, this approach has not previously been explored to identify histone PTM 'erasers', which are likely involved in weak and transient interactions.
evidence: This claim represents a knowledge gap and is based on the authors' understanding of the literature and the nature of enzyme-substrate interactions.

claim: Sirt1, Sirt2, and Sirt3 were enriched by more than 10-fold by the K4 crotonylated probe (1) in the 'selectivity filter' experiment.
source: In contrast, three nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent deacetylases (Imai et al., 2000; Landry et al., 2000; Sauve et al., 2006), Sirt1, Sirt2, and Sirt3, were enriched by more than 10-fold by the K4 crotonylated probe (1) in the 'selectivity filter' experiment (Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating that they preferentially bind to this histone Kcr mark.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, which show SILAC ratios from the CLASPI experiments.

claim: Sirt3 is likely a selective and relatively tight binding partner of H3K4Cr.
source: However, among these three selective H3K4Cr binders, only Sirt3 showed the highest SILAC ratio of H/L and thereby appeared as an outlier outside of the background in the 'affinity filter' experiment (Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1). This result indicates that Sirt3 is likely a selective and relatively tight binding partner of H3K4Cr.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the SILAC data shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, where Sirt3 shows high enrichment in both selectivity and affinity filter experiments.

claim: Recombinant Sirt3 was selectively labeled in vitro by crotonylated probe 1 (2 μM) and the labeling by probe 1 was inhibited by a H3K4Cr peptide (30 μM).
source: As shown in Figure 2C, the recombinant Sirt3 was captured by probe 1 but not by probe C, and the cross-linking was competed by the H3K4Cr peptide with an IC50=32.3 μM (Figure 2D), verifying a direct and selective interaction between Sirt3 and the K4 crotonylated H3 peptide.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2D, demonstrating selective labeling and competition.

claim: The cross-linking of Sirt3 by probe 1 was competed by the H3K4Cr peptide with an IC50=32.3 μM.
source: the cross-linking was competed by the H3K4Cr peptide with an IC50=32.3 μM (Figure 2D)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D, which shows a competition curve and IC50 determination.

claim: Sirt3 bound to the H3K4Cr peptide with Kd=25.1 μM.
source: Indeed, the direct measurement of binding affinity using isothermal titration calorimetry showed that Sirt3 bound to the H3K4Cr peptide with Kd=25.1 μM (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from isothermal titration calorimetry shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Sirt1 and 2 showed lower affinities towards the H3K4Cr peptide compared to Sirt3.
source: Consistent with our 'affinity filter' CLASPI analysis, Sirt1 and 2 showed lower affinities towards the H3K4Cr peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that they are selective but relatively weak binders towards this histone Kcr mark.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from isothermal titration calorimetry shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The crystal structure of human Sirt3 in complex with an H3K4Cr peptide was determined to 2.95 Å resolution.
source: To study the molecular basis for the recognition of H3K4Cr by Sirt3, we determined the crystal structure of human Sirt3 in complex with an H3K4Cr peptide to 2.95 Å resolution (PDB 4V1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from X-ray crystallography, with the structure deposited in the PDB.

claim: The two globular domains of Sirt3 composed of an NAD binding Rossmann fold and a zinc binding motif are similar to other sirtuins.
source: The two globular domains of Sirt3 composed of an NAD binding Rossmann fold and a zinc binding motif are similar to other sirtuins (Figure 3A) (Avalos et al., 2004; Du et al., 2011; Yuan and Marmorstein, 2012; Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3A and citations to prior structural studies of sirtuins.

claim: Residues 2RTKQTAR8 of the H3K4Cr peptide were clearly identified based on electron density.
source: Residues 2RTKQTAR8 of the H3K4Cr peptide were clearly identified based on electron density.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of electron density maps from the crystal structure.

claim: The way that the substrate is bound is similar to the published complex structure of Sirt3, with a lysine acetylated AceCS2 peptide (PDB 3GLR).
source: The way that the substrate is bound is similar to the published complex structure of Sirt3, with a lysine acetylated AceCS2 peptide (PDB 3GLR) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Jin et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and citation to Jin et al., 2009.

claim: The crotonyl lysine is located in a binding pocket formed by hydrophobic residues Phe180, Ile230, His248, Ile291, and Phe294 of Sirt3.
source: The crotonyl lysine is located in a binding pocket formed by hydrophobic residues Phe180, Ile230, His248, Ile291, and Phe294 of Sirt3 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Residue His248, a catalytic residue for the deacetylation activity of Sirt3, interacts with the crotonyl amide oxygen via hydrogen bonding in the structure.
source: Residue His248, a catalytic residue for the deacetylation activity of Sirt3, interacts with the crotonyl amide oxygen via hydrogen bonding in the structure (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3B and established knowledge about the catalytic mechanism of Sirt3.

claim: The phenyl ring of residue Phe180 aligns parallel to the planar crotonyl group and has a short distance of 3.6 Å to its conjugated carbon–carbon double bond (C=C), indicating a robust π-π stacking interaction between the two functional groups.
source: Strikingly, the phenyl ring of residue Phe180 aligns parallel to the planar crotonyl group and has a short distance of 3.6 Å to its conjugated carbon–carbon double bond (C=C) (Figure 3C, D), indicating a robust π-π stacking interaction between the two functional groups.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3C and 3D, with the inference of π-π stacking based on the observed geometry and distance.

claim: The phenylalanine residue (Phe180) of Sirt3 is conserved in Sirt1 and Sirt2, but not in other sirtuins.
source: Interestingly, a primary sequence alignment of all sirtuins revealed that the phenylalanine residue (Phe180) of Sirt3 is conserved in Sirt1 and Sirt2, but not in other sirtuins (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which may explain why Sirt4–Sirt7 were not identified in our CLASPI experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The conservation of Phe180 in Sirt1, Sirt2, and Sirt3 may explain why Sirt4–Sirt7 were not identified in the CLASPI experiments.
source: Interestingly, a primary sequence alignment of all sirtuins revealed that the phenylalanine residue (Phe180) of Sirt3 is conserved in Sirt1 and Sirt2, but not in other sirtuins (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), which may explain why Sirt4–Sirt7 were not identified in our CLASPI experiments.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the sequence alignment data and the CLASPI results.

claim: The π-π interaction between Phe180 and the crotonyl group underlies the mechanism for the recognition of crotonyl lysine by Sirt1, Sirt2, and Sirt3.
source: This π-π interaction therefore underlies the mechanism for the recognition of crotonyl lysine by Sirt1, Sirt2, and Sirt3.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the structural data showing the π-π interaction and the sequence conservation.

claim: Sirt3 efficiently catalyzed the hydrolysis of the crotonyl peptide only in the presence of NAD.
source: As expected, Sirt3 efficiently catalyzed the hydrolysis of the crotonyl peptide only in the presence of NAD (Figure 4A), suggesting an NAD-dependent decrotonylation mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 4A, which shows hydrolysis only when NAD is present.

claim: The kcat, Km, and kcat/Km for Sirt3 catalyzed decrotonylation of H3K4Cr were 0.010 s−1, 12.6 μM, and 783 s−1 M−1, respectively.
source: The steady state kinetic analysis revealed that the kcat, Km, and kcat/Km for Sirt3 catalyzed decrotonylation of H3K4Cr were 0.010 s−1, 12.6 μM, and 783 s−1 M−1, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: O-crotonyl-adenosine 5ʹ-diphosphoribose (O-Cr-ADPR) was detected as a product of the Sirt3-catalyzed hydrolysis reaction.
source: In addition, we detected O-crotonyl-adenosine 5ʹ-diphosphoribose (O-Cr-ADPR) as a product of this hydrolysis reaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A mutation of the catalytic residue (H248Y) completely abolished the decrotonylation activity of Sirt3.
source: A mutation of the catalytic residue (H248Y) that is crucial for the deacetylation activity of the enzyme also completely abolished its decrotonylation activity (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 4C, which shows no hydrolysis with the H248Y mutant.

claim: Sirt3 hydrolyzes crotonyl lysine with the same mechanism as it hydrolyzes acetyl lysine.
source: These data indicate that Sirt3 hydrolyzes crotonyl lysine with the same mechanism as it hydrolyzes acetyl lysine (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) (Tanner et al., 2000; Tanny and Moazed, 2001).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data (NAD dependence, H248Y mutation effect, O-Cr-ADPR product) and citations to prior mechanistic studies.

claim: Sirt3 manifested varied decrotonylation activities towards different crotonyl histone peptides.
source: As shown in Figure 4D–G, Sirt3 manifested varied decrotonylation activities towards these peptides and this substrate selectivity can be partially explained by the binding affinities of Sirt3 to these peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 4D-G and binding affinity data in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The substrate selectivity of Sirt3 can be partially explained by the binding affinities of Sirt3 to these peptides.
source: As shown in Figure 4D–G, Sirt3 manifested varied decrotonylation activities towards these peptides and this substrate selectivity can be partially explained by the binding affinities of Sirt3 to these peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the correlation between activity data (Figure 4D-G) and binding affinity data (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: Sirt3 binds a crotonylated peptide by recognizing both the modification site and its surrounding residues.
source: The observation that Sirt3 binds a crotonylated peptide by recognizing both the modification site and its surrounding residues was also supported by the extensive hydrophobic and hydrogen bonding interactions between Sirt3 and the peptide side chains in the Sirt3–H3K4Cr complex structure (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Sirt1 and Sirt2 also catalyzed the hydrolysis of the H3K4Cr peptide.
source: Consistent with the work of Denu and coworkers, Sirt1 and Sirt2 also catalyzed the hydrolysis of the H3K4Cr peptide, although they were relatively weaker binders towards this substrate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and is consistent with prior work by Denu and coworkers.

claim: Sirt5 or Sirt6 showed little hydrolysis of the crotonyl peptide.
source: In contrast, for Sirt5 or Sirt6, little hydrolysis of the crotonyl peptide was observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by LC-MS data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: The phenylalanine residue is only conserved in Sirt1–Sirt3.
source: These results agree well with the observation that the phenylalanine residue, which is involved in recognition of crotonyl lysine via π−π stacking interaction (Figure 3C, D), is only conserved in Sirt1–Sirt3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The catalytic efficiency of Sirt3 F180L mutant (kcat/Km=21 s−1 M−1) for the hydrolysis of the H3K4Cr peptide was about 40-fold lower than that of wild-type Sirt3.
source: The steady state kinetic data showed that the catalytic efficiency of Sirt3 F180L mutant (kcat/Km=21 s−1 M−1) for the hydrolysis of the H3K4Cr peptide was about 40-fold lower than that of wild-type Sirt3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating a critical role of the phenylalanine mediated π−π interaction in the decrotonylation activity of the enzyme.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The phenylalanine mediated π−π interaction plays a critical role in the decrotonylation activity of Sirt3.
source: The steady state kinetic data showed that the catalytic efficiency of Sirt3 F180L mutant (kcat/Km=21 s−1 M−1) for the hydrolysis of the H3K4Cr peptide was about 40-fold lower than that of wild-type Sirt3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), indicating a critical role of the phenylalanine mediated π−π interaction in the decrotonylation activity of the enzyme.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the kinetic data comparing wild-type and F180L mutant Sirt3.

claim: The F180L mutation caused only about a two-fold decrease in the deacetylation activity of Sirt3.
source: Interestingly, the F180L mutation caused only about a two-fold decrease in the deacetylation activity of the enzyme (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: The observed significant decrease in the decrotonylase activity of the F180L mutant is not caused by a potential disruption of the NAD binding pocket.
source: This result rules out the possibility that the observed significant decrease in the decrotonylase activity of the enzyme is caused by a potential disruption of the NAD binding pocket in the mutated Sirt3.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that the F180L mutation has a much smaller effect on deacetylation (which also requires NAD) than on decrotonylation.

claim: Sirt1–Sirt3 reduced global Kcr levels of all core histones.
source: Indeed, Sirt1–Sirt3 not only reduced global Kcr levels of all core histones, they also showed robust decrotonylation activity towards two known histone Kcr sites, H3K4Cr and H3K27Cr (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sirt1–Sirt3 showed robust decrotonylation activity towards two known histone Kcr sites, H3K4Cr and H3K27Cr.
source: Indeed, Sirt1–Sirt3 not only reduced global Kcr levels of all core histones, they also showed robust decrotonylation activity towards two known histone Kcr sites, H3K4Cr and H3K27Cr (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sirt1 and Sirt2 knockdowns by siRNA did not cause an appreciable increase in crotonylation levels for both the global histone and the two tested Kcr (i.e., H3K4Cr and H3K27Cr) sites.
source: Although Sirt1 and Sirt2 can decrotonylate histone peptides and proteins in vitro, their knockdowns by siRNA did not cause an appreciable increase in crotonylation levels for both the global histone and the two tested Kcr (i.e., H3K4Cr and H3K27Cr) sites (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sirt3 knockdown caused accumulation of global histone crotonylation and the H3K4Cr mark.
source: In contrast, Sirt3 knockdown caused accumulation of global histone crotonylation and the H3K4Cr mark, while the histone H3K4Ac and H3K4Me3 levels were unaltered (Figure 5C, D), suggesting that Sirt3 selectively targets histone crotonylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Sirt3 knockdown did not alter histone H3K4Ac and H3K4Me3 levels.
source: In contrast, Sirt3 knockdown caused accumulation of global histone crotonylation and the H3K4Cr mark, while the histone H3K4Ac and H3K4Me3 levels were unaltered (Figure 5C, D), suggesting that Sirt3 selectively targets histone crotonylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Sirt3 selectively targets histone crotonylation.
source: In contrast, Sirt3 knockdown caused accumulation of global histone crotonylation and the H3K4Cr mark, while the histone H3K4Ac and H3K4Me3 levels were unaltered (Figure 5C, D), suggesting that Sirt3 selectively targets histone crotonylation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observation that Sirt3 knockdown increases Kcr but not Kac or K4Me3.

claim: The crotonylation level on H3K27 was not influenced by the knockdown of Sirt3.
source: Interestingly, the crotonylation level on H3K27 was not influenced by the knockdown of Sirt3, which may be explained by the observation that Sirt3 showed weaker activity towards the H3K27Cr peptide in vitro (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data and is explained by reference to in vitro activity data.

claim: Sirt3 was found to localize predominantly to mitochondria and was mainly involved in metabolic regulations through controlling protein acetylation dynamics.
source: It should be noted that Sirt3 was found to localize predominantly to mitochondria and was mainly involved in metabolic regulations through controlling protein acetylation dynamics.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Sirt3 localization and function.

claim: Sirt3 can also be present in the nucleus in its full length form.
source: However, recent evidence has suggested that Sirt3 can also be present in the nucleus in its full length form (Scher et al., 2007; Iwahara et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scher et al., 2007 and Iwahara et al., 2012.

claim: Endogenous full length Sirt3 was detected in the nucleus of HeLa cells by both immunofluorescence and western blotting analyses.
source: Indeed, using an antibody that targets the N-terminal region of Sirt3, we detected endogenous full length Sirt3 in the nucleus of HeLa cells by both immunofluorescence and western blotting analyses (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Endogenous Sirt3 can function as an 'eraser' enzyme to regulate histone crotonylation dynamics in cells.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that endogenous Sirt3 can function as an 'eraser' enzyme to regulate histone crotonylation dynamics in cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined data showing Sirt3 nuclear localization and the effect of Sirt3 knockdown on histone crotonylation levels.

claim: Sirt3 can bind to chromatin and cause repression of the neighboring genes in U2OS cells.
source: It has been reported that Sirt3 can bind to chromatin and cause repression of the neighboring genes in U2OS cells (Iwahara et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Iwahara et al., 2012.

claim: Sirt3 knockdown resulted in significant increases in Kcr levels of five of the seven genes analyzed (Baz2a, Brip1, Ptk2, Tshz3, and Wapal).
source: As shown in Figure 5E, Sirt3 knockdown by siRNA resulted in significant increases in Kcr levels of five of the seven genes analyzed, indicating that Sirt3 may directly regulate crotonylation dynamics at the genomic loci where it binds.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Sirt3 may directly regulate crotonylation dynamics at the genomic loci where it binds.
source: As shown in Figure 5E, Sirt3 knockdown by siRNA resulted in significant increases in Kcr levels of five of the seven genes analyzed, indicating that Sirt3 may directly regulate crotonylation dynamics at the genomic loci where it binds.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the ChIP-qPCR data showing increased Kcr at specific genomic loci upon Sirt3 knockdown.

claim: The mRNA levels of three candidate genes with increased Kcr levels (Ptk2, Tshz3, and Wapal) were significantly upregulated on Sirt3 knockdown.
source: Interestingly, the mRNA levels of the three candidate genes with increased Kcr levels, Ptk2, Tshz3, and Wapal, were also significantly upregulated on Sirt3 knockdown (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Sirt3 might relieve a repressive effect on target genes through 'erasing' histone Kcr 'marks'.
source: Given that histone Kcr is enriched at active gene promoters and potential enhancers (Tan et al., 2011), this positive correlation between the gene transcription level and the nearby histone Kcr level on Sirt3 knockdown suggests that Sirt3 might relieve a repressive effect on these target genes through 'erasing' histone Kcr 'marks'.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation based on the correlation between increased Kcr and increased gene expression upon Sirt3 knockdown, combined with prior knowledge about Kcr enrichment at active promoters.

claim: The CLASPI approach overcame the difficulty of detecting weak and transient enzyme–PTM interactions by applying photo-cross-linking chemistry to convert them into irreversible covalent linkages.
source: Our CLASPI approach overcame this difficulty by applying photo-cross-linking chemistry to convert weak and transient enzyme–PTM interactions into irreversible covalent linkages, and enabled a systematic profiling of the 'erasers' of protein PTMs.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the advantages of the CLASPI approach based on the experimental design and results.

claim: The present study has largely broadened the scope of CLASPI technology from finding PTM 'readers' to identifying dynamic and transient interactions between PTMs and their 'erasers'.
source: The present study has also largely broadened the scope of CLASPI technology from finding PTM 'readers'(Li et al., 2012; Li and Kapoor, 2010), which are usually involved in relatively more stable protein–protein interactions, to identifying dynamic and transient interactions between PTMs and their 'erasers'.
evidence: This claim is an inference about the contribution of the study to the CLASPI methodology.

claim: The CLASPI approach can be used to comprehensively profile 'erasers' of other PTMs, such as arginine demethylases.
source: We anticipate that this approach can be used to comprehensively profile 'erasers' of other PTMs, such as arginine demethylases.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential future applications of the CLASPI approach.

claim: Sirtuins were initially recognized as NAD-dependent deacetylases.
source: Siruins were initially recognized as NAD-dependent deacetylases (Imai et al., 2000; Landry et al., 2000; Sauve et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations representing established scientific knowledge.

claim: Some sirtuins that displayed weak deacetylation activity had substrate specificity towards other acyl groups attached to lysine residues.
source: However, emerging evidence revealed that some sirtuins that displayed weak deacetylation activity had substrate specificity towards other acyl groups attached to lysine residues.
evidence: This represents emerging knowledge in the field about sirtuin substrate specificity.

claim: Sirt5 can preferentially hydrolyze malonyl and succinyl lysine.
source: For examples, Lin et al. recently demonstrated that Sirt5 can preferentially hydrolyze malonyl and succinyl lysine (Du et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2011), and Sirt6 can remove long chain fatty acyl groups (e.g., myristoyl group) from lysine residues (Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Du et al., 2011 and Peng et al., 2011.

claim: Sirt6 can remove long chain fatty acyl groups (e.g., myristoyl group) from lysine residues.
source: For examples, Lin et al. recently demonstrated that Sirt5 can preferentially hydrolyze malonyl and succinyl lysine (Du et al., 2011; Peng et al., 2011), and Sirt6 can remove long chain fatty acyl groups (e.g., myristoyl group) from lysine residues (Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jiang et al., 2013.

claim: The newly discovered decrotonylase activity broadens the landscape of PTMs that are targeted by sirtuins.
source: This newly discovered decrotonylase activity broadens the landscape of PTMs that are targeted by sirtuins, and it also provides new impetus to investigate the cellular mechanisms and functions of Sirt1–Sirt3, which to date have been considered solely as deacetylases.
evidence: This is an inference about the significance of the findings for understanding sirtuin biology.

claim: The finding provides new impetus to investigate the cellular mechanisms and functions of Sirt1–Sirt3, which to date have been considered solely as deacetylases.
source: This newly discovered decrotonylase activity broadens the landscape of PTMs that are targeted by sirtuins, and it also provides new impetus to investigate the cellular mechanisms and functions of Sirt1–Sirt3, which to date have been considered solely as deacetylases.
